viral_ticker_tweets.full_text_en:
Remarks from Anthropic CEO @DarioAmodei on our initial public offering:

My co-founders and I started Anthropic because we believe that the most powerful technology of our time should be built for the benefit of humankind.

Daniela and I lost our father to a disease that, just a few years later, became curable. I started my career in biology, hoping to help future cures come sooner. In the lab, I saw the vast thicket of complexity that scientists face when they’re trying to understand disease and develop new treatments.

So many of the scientific tools that can cut through that thicket—tools for gene editing, gene synthesis, controlling brain cells with light—started as pure ideas. In other words, they came from thinking. From intelligence.

Human intelligence has already made diseases like plague, smallpox, and polio history for most of the world. But progress on other diseases has been too slow for so many patients and their families. Going from a great idea to a treatment can take decades: it took many years from the first discovery of a strange repeating pattern in DNA to the approval of the first treatment for a disease using CRISPR.

Nature is full of these patterns. But we’ve had too little intelligence to decipher most of them; too few scientists, with too little time. Now we can build that intelligence. Whether it’s protein folding, drug design, cancer genetics, or clinical trial administration, scientists across many areas of biology and medicine are finding Claude can help them do their research in a fraction of the time it would’ve taken just a couple of years ago. I believe sufficiently powerful AI, working in concert with humans, could compress a century of scientific and medical progress into a decade.

I don’t want to get ahead of myself. At this point all we have are early results. Experiments and clinical trials will still take time. And although they involve slow and ponderous processes, I believe those processes can be substantially accelerated by AI. We hope that in the future fewer families miss a cure by just a few years.

Medicine is just a particularly vivid example, but there are many others. Our customers—the world’s most ambitious companies, nonprofits, and individual people—are already applying the intelligence we’ve built to stimulate economic growth; lift people out of poverty; protect democracy and free societies; even make everyday services like the DMV work better. We’re proud to work alongside them. And I’m extremely optimistic about what we can do together in the future.

At the same time, we have always been honest that this technology has very real risks. These range from misuse of the technology by individuals or nation-states, to economic disruption, to losing control of AI systems. We discuss these risks not because we think they are inevitable, but because we think they are avoidable.

Avoiding them depends on the choices made by the people building AI. There is a gigantic difference between how AI will go if we pay little attention to safety, versus how it will go if we are obsessed with safety. And an obsession with safety and with public benefit has been woven into Anthropic’s DNA from the start. From safeguards against biological and cyber risks, to alignment training and testing, to looking inside our models like an X-ray, Anthropic has pioneered methods for understanding and steering the behavior of AI systems.

There is much work still to be done, and the most difficult safety work lies ahead of us. The incredible talent of the company that has enabled us to build the most capable AI systems will need to be directed, even more so than it has already, towards double- and triple-checking that those AI systems are safe and secure.

And to state it unequivocally, we will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control. We will not bend to either business or political pressure. Today puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing.

If we can show it’s possible to make the right choices on safety and still build an incredibly successful company, others in our industry will be inspired to do the same. We call this a race to the top. When the race to the top is working properly, it doesn’t matter which company has the best models—everyone wins because everyone is building safely. The race to the top works best when driven from the front of the pack, and we fully hope and expect to do so, but the goal is to make the whole industry better, regardless of whether Anthropic is winning or losing at any given time.

The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history, and we have a rare opportunity to shape it for the better.

This moment is bigger than any one company, or any one country. It will take all of us, working together, to ensure this technology goes well for us and the many generations to come. Starting today, we hope that you’ll join us on this mission.
viral_ticker_tweets.full_text_zh:
Anthropic 首席执行官 @DarioAmodei 关于我们首次公开募股的评论：

我和我的联合创始人创立了 Anthropic，因为我们相信我们这个时代最强大的技术应该是为了造福人类而构建的。

丹妮拉和我的父亲因一种疾病去世，仅仅几年后，这种疾病就可以治愈。我的职业生涯始于生物学，希望能帮助未来的治愈方法早日到来。在实验室里，我看到了科学家在试图了解疾病和开发新疗法时所面临的巨大复杂性。

许多能够突破这一困境的科学工具——基因编辑、基因合成、用光控制脑细胞的工具——都是从纯粹的想法开始的。换句话说，它们来自于思考。来自智力。

人类智慧已经让世界上大部分地区的鼠疫、天花和脊髓灰质炎等疾病成为历史。但对于如此多的患者及其家人来说，其他疾病的进展太慢了。从一个伟大的想法到一种治疗方法可能需要数十年的时间：从首次发现 DNA 中奇怪的重复模式到第一个使用 CRISPR 治疗疾病的方法获得批准，花了很多年的时间。

大自然充满了这些模式。但我们的智慧太少，无法破译其中的大部分。科学家太少，时间太少。现在我们可以构建这种智能。无论是蛋白质折叠、药物设计、癌症遗传学还是临床试验管理，生物学和医学许多领域的科学家都发现克劳德可以帮助他们完成研究，所需时间只是几年前的一小部分。我相信足够强大的人工智能，与人类协同工作，可以将一个世纪的科学和医学进步压缩为十年。

我不想超越自己。目前我们所拥有的只是早期结果。实验和临床试验仍需要时间。尽管它们涉及缓慢而繁重的过程，但我相信人工智能可以大大加速这些过程。我们希望未来能有更少的家庭因仅仅几年的时间而错过治疗。

医学只是一个特别生动的例子，但还有很多其他例子。我们的客户——世界上最雄心勃勃的公司、非营利组织和个人——已经在应用我们构建的智能来刺激经济增长；让人们摆脱贫困；保护民主和自由社会；甚至让 DMV 等日常服务更好地运作。我们很自豪能与他们一起工作。我对我们未来可以一起做的事情非常乐观。

与此同时，我们一直诚实地认为这项技术存在非常现实的风险。这些问题包括个人或民族国家滥用技术、经济混乱、失去对人工智能系统的控制等。我们讨论这些风险不是因为我们认为它们是不可避免的，而是因为我们认为它们是可以避免的。

避免它们取决于构建人工智能的人们做出的选择。如果我们不关心安全，人工智能将会如何发展，而如果我们痴迷于安全，人工智能将会如何发展，两者之间存在着巨大的差异。对安全和公共利益的痴迷从一开始就融入了 Anthropic 的基因中。从防范生物和网络风险，到校准训练和测试，再到像 X 射线一样观察我们的模型，Anthropic 开创了理解和引导人工智能系统行为的方法。

任重而道远，最艰巨的安全工作还在后面。该公司拥有令人难以置信的人才，使我们能够构建最强大的人工智能系统，我们需要对其进行双重和三重检查，以确保这些人工智能系统的安全性，甚至比现在更加努力。

明确地说，我们将加快人工智能系统的训练和部署步伐，只要有必要，我们就确信它们是安全的，并将继续处于人类控制之下。我们不会屈服于商业或政治压力。今天，公司的财务状况变得更加强大，这样做只会增强我们做正确事情的决心。

如果我们能够证明我们可以在安全方面做出正确的选择，同时仍能打造一家极其成功的公司，那么我们行业的其他人也会受到启发，采取同样的做法。我们称之为登顶竞赛。当竞争顺利进行时，哪家公司拥有最好的模型并不重要——每个人都会赢，因为每个人都在安全地建造。当处于领先地位时，通往顶峰的竞争效果最好，我们完全希望并期望这样做，但目标是让整个行业变得更好，无论 Anthropic 在任何特定时间是赢还是输。

机器智能的出现是人类历史上的开创性时刻之一，我们有一个难得的机会来让它变得更好。

这一刻比任何一家公司或任何一个国家都重要。我们所有人都需要共同努力，才能确保这项技术为我们和子孙后代带来良好的发展。从今天开始，我们希望您能加入我们的行列。

viral_ticker_tweets.full_text_en:
I came across an interesting finding in yesterday’s @databricks announcement.

After studying more than 80,000 customer pipeline issues, the company found that over half required knowledge specific to the organization to resolve.

And I think there’s a much bigger business lesson hiding in that number.

When we talk about AI agents, we often focus on what they can do.

Can they write content?

Can they analyze data?

Can they manage workflows?

Can they complete tasks without constant human involvement?

Those are useful questions.

But there’s another one I find increasingly important as we build CAIS.

Does the agent actually understand the business it’s working for?

Imagine two companies using exactly the same AI tools.

One wants to increase sales as quickly as possible.

The other is prioritizing profitability, customer retention and protecting its brand positioning.

An agent might recommend the same aggressive discount campaign to both.

The recommendation could be technically sound.

But it wouldn’t necessarily be right for both businesses.

That’s the difference between having access to information and understanding business context.

It’s also why we’re building CAIS around the idea of One Brand Brain.

The goal is to bring business strategy, knowledge, people and AI workflows into a more coherent operating environment.

Not because every decision should be automated.

Quite the opposite.

Because businesses need to know which decisions can be delegated, which require additional context and which should remain firmly in human hands.

I think we’ll see increasingly capable agents over the coming months.

But capability alone won’t determine which businesses benefit most.

The companies that understand their own processes, priorities and decision-making responsibilities will be in a much stronger position to use that capability effectively.

Sometimes the most valuable thing you can give an AI agent isn’t another tool.

It’s a better understanding of the business.
viral_ticker_tweets.full_text_zh:
我在昨天的@databricks 公告中发现了一个有趣的发现。

在研究了 80,000 多个客户渠道问题后，该公司发现超过一半的问题需要组织特有的知识来解决。

我认为这个数字中隐藏着更大的商业教训。

当我们谈论人工智能代理时，我们经常关注它们能做什么。

他们可以写内容吗？

他们可以分析数据吗？

他们可以管理工作流程吗？

它们能否在没有人类持续参与的情况下完成任务？

这些都是有用的问题。

但我发现，随着我们建立 CAIS，还有一个问题变得越来越重要。

代理人是否真正了解其所从事的业务？

想象一下两家公司使用完全相同的人工智能工具。

人们希望尽快增加销售额。

另一个是优先考虑盈利能力、客户保留和保护其品牌定位。

代理商可能会向两者推荐相同的激进折扣活动。

该建议在技术上可能是合理的。

但这不一定适合两家企业。

这就是获取信息和了解业务环境之间的区别。

这也是我们围绕同一个品牌大脑的理念构建 CAIS 的原因。

目标是将业务战略、知识、人员和人工智能工作流程带入一个更加一致的操作环境中。

并不是因为每个决定都应该自动化。

恰恰相反。

因为企业需要知道哪些决策可以委托，哪些需要额外的背景信息，哪些应该牢牢掌握在人手中。

我认为在接下来的几个月里我们会看到能力越来越强的特工。

但仅凭能力并不能决定哪些企业受益最多。

了解自己的流程、优先事项和决策责任的公司将能够更有效地利用这种能力。

有时，你能为人工智能代理提供的最有价值的东西并不是其他工具。

这是对业务的更好理解。

top_three.summary_en: Singapore-based DayOne Data Centers has shelved its planned US IPO amid cooling market valuations for AI infrastructure and intensifying regulatory scrutiny. Despite efforts to navigate the AI compute demand surge, the company faces significant headwinds from investor skepticism regarding data center asset sustainability and strict US regulations on the export of advanced AI hardware to entities with China-linked operations.
paragraphs: SINGAPORE – DayOne Data Centers has put plans for its multibillion-dollar US initial public offering on hold, sources familiar with the matter said, as investors question the sustainability of frothy valuations for digital infrastructure supporting the artificial intelligence boom.
But it started to reassess options including a delay or a smaller listing as volatility increased around data centres and AI stocks.
Singapore-based DayOne may still pursue an IPO in 2027 if the situation and market sentiment improves, the sources said, asking not to be identified because the information is not public.
The company filed for the IPO in October and has been working with Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Citigroup and BNP Paribas on the listing.
Deliberations are ongoing and no final decisions on the IPO have been made, the sources said.
A representative for DayOne declined to comment.
Doubts about the potential payoff from massive investments into AI have fuelled volatility in global markets.
The Nasdaq 100 has dropped more than 6% in November, heading for its worst November performance since 2008.
Still, Anthropic staged a record-breaking US$107.3 billion IPO and private placement and rose 17% on its trading debut on Nov 19, becoming the world’s seventh-most valuable company.
Other data centre-related companies have either pulled or delayed their IPO plans amid investor concerns in the sector.

In October, Firmus Grid abandoned its attempt at one of Australia’s biggest-ever initial public offerings, while Blackstone-backed AirTrunk is delaying a listing of a real estate investment trust in Singapore until 2027.

The US in November put interim rules on those four countries to restrict China’s access to advanced AI chips and servers, telling data centre operators they will need a license to purchase American tech hardware.

top_three.author: 9to5Google
top_three.content_snippet:
After the better part of 7 years, Samsung’s mobile division has a new chief and it’s Choi Won-Joon, who is already off to a great start with the successful launch of Galaxy Z Fold 8.

In an announcement today, Samsung confirmed some shuffling of its executive team, most notably with the end of TM Roh’s tenure as the head of Samsung’s MX business unit. In other words, there’s a new captain at the helm for Samsung’s mobile division, and it’s Choi Won-Joon.

Won-Joon has been the Chief Operating Of
top_three.summary_en: Samsung Electronics has announced a leadership transition in its MX (Mobile Experience) business unit, appointing Chief Operating Officer Choi Won-Joon as the new head of the mobile division to oversee post-Galaxy S26 and Z Fold 8 product strategy. TM Roh will step down from the mobile leadership role but will retain his position as Samsung Electronics co-CEO, focusing on broader corporate strategy and cross-divisional integration.

topic_focus.title_zh: Anthropic万亿估值IPO引发全球科技股集体跳水

topic_focus.summary_zh: Anthropic以1.5万亿美元估值在纳斯达克挂牌，引发资本市场对AI泡沫的恐慌性重估。尽管Iconiq资本获得超4倍回报，但软银、台积电等亚洲巨头股价因对AI不可持续的高估值担忧而剧烈波动，市值蒸发规模空前。
topic_focus.summary_en: Anthropic’s $1.5 trillion Nasdaq debut ignited a violent market revaluation. While Iconiq Capital secured a 430%+ return, the euphoria triggered massive sell-offs in Asian giants like SoftBank and TSMC, as investors scrambled to hedge against unsustainable AI valuations and potential bubble bursts.

perspective_pro.point_en: Argue that Anthropic is not just a model vendor but the infrastructure for global productivity, justifying a trillion-dollar valuation as a necessary entry price for controlling the AGI era.

perspective_con.speaker_zh: 华尔街金融分析师与避险基金经理
perspective_con.speaker_en: Wall Street analysts and hedge fund managers
perspective_con.point_zh: 指出AI模型商业化落地远未支撑如此恐怖的市盈率，Anthropic IPO背后的资本狂欢已脱离基本面，高估值将加速二级市场抛售并对供应链上下游产生反噬。
perspective_con.point_en: Critique the astronomical P/E ratios that ignore current commercial realities; they view the IPO as a dangerous bubble that threatens to drain liquidity from the broader hardware and chip supply chain.

不准确完全不会产生任何后果，并且每一个夸大其辞的动机都可以，并且 x 算法已针对此进行了调整

when scrolling social media i think it is worth bearing in mind that you can say “odds of reaching SOTA have dropped to zero” and get alot of likes and then 3 months later when they have reached SOTA you post apology form and get even more likes and the subject of your writing prints it out and thanks you for motivation

theres no consequences at all for inaccuracy and every incentive for hyperbole and the x algorithm is tuned for this

topic_focus.summary_zh: 黄仁勋因婚外情丑闻意外辞去英伟达CEO职务，加州总检察长随即对公司发起司法调查。此事件叠加俄籍间谍窃取国防科技情报的阴云，令英伟达深陷监管与信誉旋涡，股价较近期高点已回调近40%。

news.author: Search Engine Roundtable
news.content_snippet:
Google is now officially rolling out what it calls the "collapsible sidebar" within Google Search. We spotted this a few weeks ago and we called it then the AI Mode sidebar in Google Search. Robby Stein from Google said "New on the Google desktop homepage globally: we’re rolling out a collapsible sidebar to easily find & jump back into your recent AI searches."

Robby Stein posted a video of this on X and wrote, "People are coming to Search with more questions that aren’t just one and done – and
news.summary_en: Google has officially rolled out a collapsible sidebar on its desktop Search homepage, a strategic move by its search experience division to enhance continuity for users engaged in multi-turn AI queries. The feature is designed to shift search patterns from one-off interactions toward long-term engagement by providing a persistent hub for recent AI-generated tasks.

news.summary_en: Singapore-based DayOne Data Centers has shelved its planned US IPO amid cooling market valuations for AI infrastructure and intensifying regulatory scrutiny. Despite efforts to navigate the AI compute demand surge, the company faces significant headwinds from investor skepticism regarding data center asset sustainability and strict US regulations on the export of advanced AI hardware to entities with China-linked operations.
paragraphs: SINGAPORE – DayOne Data Centers has put plans for its multibillion-dollar US initial public offering on hold, sources familiar with the matter said, as investors question the sustainability of frothy valuations for digital infrastructure supporting the artificial intelligence boom.
But it started to reassess options including a delay or a smaller listing as volatility increased around data centres and AI stocks.
Singapore-based DayOne may still pursue an IPO in 2027 if the situation and market sentiment improves, the sources said, asking not to be identified because the information is not public.
The company filed for the IPO in October and has been working with Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Citigroup and BNP Paribas on the listing.
Deliberations are ongoing and no final decisions on the IPO have been made, the sources said.
A representative for DayOne declined to comment.
Doubts about the potential payoff from massive investments into AI have fuelled volatility in global markets.
The Nasdaq 100 has dropped more than 6% in November, heading for its worst November performance since 2008.
Still, Anthropic staged a record-breaking US$107.3 billion IPO and private placement and rose 17% on its trading debut on Nov 19, becoming the world’s seventh-most valuable company.
Other data centre-related companies have either pulled or delayed their IPO plans amid investor concerns in the sector.

In October, Firmus Grid abandoned its attempt at one of Australia’s biggest-ever initial public offerings, while Blackstone-backed AirTrunk is delaying a listing of a real estate investment trust in Singapore until 2027.

The US in November put interim rules on those four countries to restrict China’s access to advanced AI chips and servers, telling data centre operators they will need a license to purchase American tech hardware.
DayOne’s backers include Coatue, Hillhouse, GDS Holdings, SoftBank Vision Fund and Citadel’s Ken Griffin. BLOOMBERG

news.title: This 16-Year-Old Founded an AI Missile Startup. He’s Targeting ‘Cost per Kill’
news.title_en: This 16-Year-Old Founded an AI Missile Startup. He’s Targeting ‘Cost per Kill’
news.author: Joel Khalili
news.summary_en:
At 16 years old, Henrijs Dandzbergs is too young to vote. Or drink. Or smoke. Or drive unsupervised. But he’s not too young to win half a million dollars for his AI-guided-missile startup.

paragraphs: At 16 years old, Henrijs Dandzbergs is too young to vote. Or drink. Or smoke. Or drive unsupervised. But he’s not too young to win half a million dollars for his AI-guided-missile startup.

In September, Dandzbergs, who was born in Latvia, was admitted to Y Combinator’s fall 2026 cohort. The startup accelerator counts companies like Airbnb, Stripe, DoorDash, and Reddit among its alumni; Dandzbergs is likely the youngest solo founder in its vaunted history.

His startup, Polemos Industries, is attempting to develop a new class of precision-guided missile that can be easily and cheaply manufactured, can be fired from portable launchers, and can resist jamming attempts. “I think missiles are the coolest thing,” Dandzbergs tells WIRED. “A lot of people that have found success in engineering early on have had a passion for blowing stuff up.”

In conversation, Dandzbergs is poised and articulate. He talks about “attacking hard problems,” breaking things down to “first principles,” and how the Ukraine conflict has forever altered the theater of war—a personal fixation, given his country's proximity to Russia. He projects an unassailable confidence in his own abilities.
“He’s a pretty exceptional person,” says Harj Taggar, a YC partner assigned to mentor Dandzbergs. “I’m still somewhat in disbelief that we’re talking about a 16-year-old.”

Dandzbergs has resolved to apply these unusual talents to figuring out how to optimize targeted killing. His startup’s guiding ambition, according to its investor one-pager, is to bring down the “cost per kill.”

As a young(er) kid, Dandzbergs was rarely in one place for long; his family moved between Latvia, Indonesia, Australia, and Spain. His surfer father, part owner of an insurance company, likes to go wherever he might find the raddest waves.

Early in his schooling, which mostly took place online, Dandzbergs demonstrated a clear talent for science and math. His room started to look like a lab, littered with schematics, robotics, Raspberry Pis, and 3D-printed components.

When Covid struck, Dandzbergs’ family returned to Latvia. His parents enrolled him in Astra Nova, an Elon Musk–linked school where students undergo an experimental curriculum built around lateral thinking and problem-solving instead of rote memorization. Dandzbergs took a class taught by a NASA employee and became fascinated by aerospace engineering. His lab creations became ever more elaborate: a bionic arm, a thermal control system for a model rocket, sensors for a self-flying drone.

Around this time, Russia invaded Ukraine. In Latvia, Dandzbergs started to see military jets overhead, and stray missiles were intercepted at the Russian border. With the sovereignty of Eastern European nations under threat, new defense startups began to pop up across the region. Dandzbergs wanted in.
“A patriotic intention to protect my country, European countries, and Ukrainian and American soldiers, and understanding the future of autonomous warfare—that’s my drive,” he says.
To stretch his technical skills, Dandzbergs started to take part in hackathons, where software and hardware engineers compete to develop the most sophisticated prototype from scratch.

In April of this year, he flew to London to take part in a hackathon held by Unicorn Mafia, an invitation-only group of developers. The prize included $10,000 in cash, a plane ticket to San Francisco, and free legal assistance with O-1 visa applications to stay in the US.

Less than 48 hours later, Dandzbergs and his two teammates, Aleksandrs Tihenko and Kai Yang, had built an AI system that could design hardware circuit boards from natural language prompts, much like how a software engineer might use AI to generate code. Though his teammates are both a few years older, Dandzbergs pushed for them to include even more intricate features in the prototype. “It was amazing,” says Tihenko. “The imagination of Henrijs in the hardware space is just crazy.”

Seeing that they stood no chance of beating Dandzbergs’ group and other front-runners, teams started to drop out of the competition, according to Fergus McKenzie-Wilson, Unicorn Mafia’s director and one of the hackathon judges. “What they built was incredibly impressive,” he says. “No one had ever seen that before.”
When the organizers crowned Dandzbergs’ team victorious, somebody handed him the mic. “I’m 16 years old,” he said.

The week after the hackathon, Dandzbergs and his teammates pitched their circuit board concept to YC. They won a place in the summer program, but Dandzbergs wavered over whether he should drop out of high school. The trio also sparred over whether the startup should focus on applying the technology to the defense sector, Dandzbergs’ primary area of interest. Dandzbergs ended up pulling out of the partnership. “It was hard,” says Tihenko. “But ultimately we just settled that the best decision for the company would be to part ways and focus on different things.”

By the summer, Danzbergs was set on building a defense startup and reapplied to YC on his own. He had spotted a gap in the market, he claimed, for AI-guided missiles that were more precise and could carry bigger warheads than the drones deployed widely in Ukraine. His products, he added, would be cheaper and easier to manufacture than hulking great rocket systems.

YC initially tried to steer him away. Dandzbergs was promising a lot of everything, all at once. It wasn’t clear whether his idea could work or whether pulling out of school was the right thing for him to do. “There’s a paternal element to it,” says Taggar. “You don’t want to be screwing up people's lives—and working on a startup is a pretty serious thing.”

Dandzbergs is up against a fleet of defense companies—from Anduril to CoAspire to Leidos—aiming to develop cheaper, mass-producible missiles. The more sophisticated the guidance system, the more difficult that task becomes.

“You can build a cheap missile that doesn’t go very far. You can build a cheap missile that doesn’t carry much of a payload. You can build a cheap missile that has a low reliability rate,” says Tom Karako, director of the Missile Defense Project and senior fellow at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. “There are trade-offs.”

But Dandzbergs wasn’t going to be dissuaded, and YC figured that somebody else would probably invest in his idea. The incubator invited him to join its fall program. “Big picture, you never know if these things are possible or not,” says Taggar. “Is it a non-zero-percent chance that it could be possible? That’s frankly the threshold, especially if it’s a really big [idea].”

So far, according to Dandzbergs, Polemos Industries has developed the software system that will guide its missiles and has begun to hammer out elements of the hardware design. By the time the YC program finishes in December, he hopes to be able to showcase a prototype missile.

If he does ultimately succeed, though, Dandzbergs will need to confront an assortment of hairy ethical quandaries. Who should have access to these new missiles? What if a technical error were to result in friendly fire? Can he make peace with his technology being used to end somebody’s life?
Dandzbergs claims that he has come to terms with these issues. He says he takes solace in the belief that his motivations are pure: to protect the US and its European allies.

By his logic, autonomous weapons are an inevitable part of the future, so he might as well be the one who builds them. “I choose not to shy away from the emergence of modern conflict as a global issue. I simply don’t have a lot of respect for people that do,” he says. “I want to be part of it. I want to move with the future of warfare.”
But others who have found themselves in a similar position say it’s difficult to know in advance how somebody will deal with the knowledge that their invention has killed people.

McKenzie-Wilson, the Unicorn Mafia director, launched a drone startup in his early twenties. Initially, he had meant for the drones to evacuate wounded soldiers, but after a missile company invested, his startup retooled its technology to drop payloads too. He left around the same time.
“I don’t think I was emotionally mature enough,” he says. “[Dandzbergs] will realize at some point. He’ll either have an issue with it or he won’t.”

Polemos Industries announced itself publicly on November 5 with a glossy social media video. Set to the ticking of a clock, it featured a set of four missiles fired into the sky from ground launchers, then blowing a convoy of four military vehicles to smithereens.

The video climbed to the top of the trending page on X. In the responses, a couple of people tagged Palmer Luckey, cofounder of Anduril, who was 19 when he started his first company. “Coming for him,” Dandzbergs responded.

Dandzbergs recognizes that people are likely to dismiss him for his age. But he considers youth one of his biggest advantages. “Please don’t say I’m sacrificing my childhood,” he says. “This is the childhood I dreamed of.”

Those chips sit in Nscale’s data center in Glomfjord, Norway. The setup is a rental, not a sale, so the hardware stays put while the customer taps the computing power remotely.

That one customer was a very big deal for Nscale’s finances. The company generated $33 million in revenue in 2025, and ByteDance’s unit, referred to as Spring, accounted for approximately $24 million of it.
That works out to approximately 73% of the year’s revenue from a single client.
The contract also played a key role in Nscale securing a $105 million loan from Macquarie.
That loan came with strings attached. It included requirements for export-control compliance monitoring, reflecting rising regulatory pressure on tech companies with ties to China.

paragraphs: BrightAI Inc., a startup that helps industrial companies detect malfunctioning equipment, has raised $97 million in funding.

Smith Point Capital led the Series A round. BrightAI said in its Wednesday announcement of the deal that a number of other venture capital firms contributed as well. They were joined by GE Vernova Inc., an energy equipment company that emerged from the 2024 split-up of General Electric Co.

Many industrial machinery malfunctions affect internal components that aren’t visible to an outside observer. As a result, issues often go unnoticed until they cause a major disruption. Palo Alto, California-based BrightAI develops hardware and software tools that help customers spot issues earlier.

The first component of the company’s product portfolio is a collection of sensors called State Stickers. They’re small, rectangular devices with a ruggedized case and a long battery life. Technicians can attach them to industrial equipment to monitor for issues that can’t be detected visually.

The motion of a machine’s internal components produces noise and vibrations that tend to follow a specific pattern. If an industrial fan’s blades rotate 30 times per minute, it might give off a whooshing sound every two seconds. BrightAI’s State Stickers can detect when a machine diverges from its usual operating pattern.

The sensors wirelessly transmit their measurements to a device called the Stateful AI Hub. It runs artificial intelligence models that analyze the data for signs of hardware failures. According to the company, its models become more accurate as the number of sensors deployed at a site grows.

BrightAI offers software that enables companies to augment the data from its sensors with drone footage. A utility, for example, could use a BrightAI-powered drone to detect erosion at the top of an electric pole. The company’s AI models automatically draw a square around damaged components to spare technicians the hassle of manually analyzing footage.

The company says that its software can also collect maintenance data in other ways. A BrightAI-powered drone can read the meters that are attached to assets such as data center coolant tanks to check their internal pressure. Furthermore, built-in support for infrared cameras enables the software to spot overheating equipment.

The third core component of BrightAI’s product portfolio is an AI wearable. The Stateful Wearable, as it’s called, provides technicians with troubleshooting advice in the field. It also checks whether they follow safety guidelines during inspections and automatically turns maintenance data into reports.

“Our infrastructure is under more strain than it has ever been, and Physical AI has finally become reliable enough to work in the field,” said founder and Chief Executive Alex Hawkinson. “Bringing those two facts together is a once-in-a-generation opportunity.”

BrightAI says that its products monitor hundreds of thousands of industrial assets across 50,000 sites. Investor GE Vernova, which is also a customer, plans to expand its use of the company’s technology in connection with this week’s funding round. BrightAI, for its part, will use the capital to grow its international presence.

news.content_snippet:
Technology stocks in Asia fell on Friday as Anthropic’s record listing in New York rattled the region’s equity markets and failed to reverse losses from a deepening sell-off in AI companies.

Shares of SoftBank, which holds a roughly 13 per cent stake in OpenAI, sank more than 15 per cent, while Japan’s Nikkei 225 index shed nearly 5 per cent.

Taiwan’s main stock index is set for its worst week since 1991 as it dropped almost 18 per cent and shed more than $500bn in market capitalisation.

paragraphs: Technology stocks in Asia fell on Friday as Anthropic’s record listing in New York rattled the region’s equity markets and failed to reverse losses from a deepening sell-off in AI companies.
Shares of SoftBank, which holds a roughly 13 per cent stake in OpenAI, sank more than 15 per cent, while Japan’s Nikkei 225 index shed nearly 5 per cent.
Taiwan’s main stock index is set for its worst week since 1991 as it dropped almost 18 per cent and shed more than $500bn in market capitalisation.
The declines came after Anthropic raised $81bn in the world’s biggest-ever initial public offering.
The Claude AI maker’s stock closed 17 per cent above its IPO price on Thursday, but the Nasdaq 100 ended 2.2 per cent lower.

Futures pointed to the index falling another 1 per cent when Wall Street opens on Friday. Anthropic shares declined almost 5 per cent in after-market trading but remain up more than 11 per cent from its IPO price.
Some investors interpreted Anthropic’s listing as a signal that a bull run in AI stocks was drawing to a close.
“Normally, the biggest IPOs are done at the peak of the market, not at the bottom,” said Hao Hong, chief investment officer for Lotus Asset Management.
Albert Saporta, group chief executive of asset manager GAM Holding, noted Anthropic’s IPO was “priced 25 per cent below the valuations of a few weeks ago”.
“This monstrous capex binge with nobody having a sense of the return on investment is unravelling,” he said.

John Woods, chief investment officer for Asia at Lombard Odier, argued that declines in Asia showed investors were shifting their emphasis away from hardware suppliers such as the chipmakers and towards AI software developers such as Anthropic.
“Anthropic’s IPO was pretty strong,” he said. “Asia’s drop shows the AI trade maturing.”
The declines in Asia mark a sharp reversal for what had been some of the world’s best performers since the start of 2025.

The unceremonious departure of Jensen Huang from Nvidia and the prospect of tightening US restrictions on chip exports had already dented investor sentiment for the region’s chipmakers, crucial to the global AI data centre build-out.
“This trade has been very narrow and very levered,” said Ecaterina Bigos, senior markets strategist at BNP Paribas Asset Management. “At the moment the market is deleveraging whatever they can.”

paragraphs: Anthropic PBC shares were down about 5% in post-market trading as the artificial intelligence developer wrapped up its first day as a public company after a record-setting $107.3 billion offering.

The late moves pared a debut pop of 17% on Thursday, which provided a rare bright spot as the Nasdaq fell 2.2%. The broader market continued on a downward trend into the Asian day, with global stocks poised for their longest losing streak in more than three years, as the AI trade cratered.

While the bright open for the Claude chatbot maker reflected massive investor appetite after a heavily oversubscribed initial public offering, the late slide underscored the volatility facing tech megacaps amidst shifting expectations for enterprise software monetization and high capital expenditure.

Anthropic priced its offering at $83 a share, above an already elevated target range, raising more than $8.1 billion in new proceeds. Backed by major technology giants including Amazon.com Inc. and Alphabet Inc., the company has emerged alongside OpenAI as a linchpin of generative AI infrastructure.

Trading in Anthropic's shares drew intense scrutiny across Wall Street as analysts evaluated whether monumental frontier model development and GPU computing costs can yield sustained profitability. The IPO represents the largest venture-backed tech listing in history, surpassing previous records set by high-profile cloud and social media debuts.

周四的尾盘走势回吐了 17% 的首日涨幅，为纳斯达克指数下跌 2.2% 提供了难得的亮点。随着人工智能交易的暴跌，大盘继续呈下跌趋势，进入亚洲交易日，全球股市将出现三年多以来最长的连续下跌。
虽然 Claude 聊天机器人开发商在开盘时的强劲表现反映了经历严重超额认购后投资者的巨大热情，但尾盘的回落凸显了大型科技企业面临的市场波动——在企业级软件商业化变现与庞大资本开支周期的交织下，市场情绪正经历剧烈博弈。
Anthropic 将 IPO 发行价定为每股 83 美元，高于此前已上调的指导区间上限，单笔募资超 81 亿美元。在亚马逊（Amazon.com Inc.）与 Alphabet Inc. 等科技巨头的巨额注资背书下，Anthropic 已与 OpenAI 并列成为全球生成式 AI 基础设施的核心支柱。
Anthropic 的挂牌交易引发了华尔街投行的全方位审视，分析师聚焦于前沿大模型研发与 GPU 算力集群的庞大资本开支能否转化为可持续的盈利能力。此次上市创下了全球风险投资支持科技企业史上规模最大的 IPO 纪录，打破了此前所有云计算与移动互联网巨头保持的公开发行市值高度。

WASHINGTON, Nov 19 (Reuters) - White House national cyber director Sean Cairncross was "fired" from his job, a person close to the White House said on Thursday, days after technology outages disrupted US air travel, banking and national security systems.

The ouster comes as US President Donald Trump and his administration face mounting scrutiny over their response to the series of disruptions over the past week, including a global outage affecting hundreds of millions of Microsoft users and a n
news.summary_en: President Donald Trump dismissed National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross, with DoD CIO Kirsten Davies serving as interim lead. The move follows widespread technical outages that crippled U.S. air travel and banking sectors, prompting intense legislative scrutiny over the administration's crisis response capabilities.
paragraphs: WASHINGTON, Nov 19 (Reuters) - White House national cyber director Sean Cairncross was "fired" from his job, a person close to the White House said on Thursday, days after technology outages disrupted US air travel, banking and national security systems.

The ouster comes as US President Donald Trump and his administration face mounting scrutiny over their response to the series of disruptions over the past week, including a global outage affecting hundreds of millions of Microsoft users and a nationwide halt to air travel that disrupted more than 18,000 flights.
The dismissal of Cairncross dismissal is the administration's first major personnel move since the outages.

Cairncross oversaw cybersecurity policy and strategy across the federal government. Department of Defense Chief Information Officer Kirsten Davies will assume the position temporarily, according to the source.
"The president fully supported firing Sean Cairncross from his position," said the person, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
Cairncross said in a statement on Thursday night it was the "honor of a lifetime to serve" in Trump's administration.

The recent technology disruptions are likely linked to corporate efforts to rapidly patch newly discovered software vulnerabilities in the AI age, cybersecurity experts told Reuters. Advanced AI tools make it easier for companies to uncover weaknesses in their cybersecurity protections.
The top US intelligence official said on Wednesday the disruptions were separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes and not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.

Republican Senator Josh Hawley of Missouri on Tuesday told reporters in Washington the Trump administration should brief lawmakers on the outages so they can "share with the American people what's happening here."

Cairncross was an executive at the Republican National Committee before assuming the cyber director role. His successor will need to be confirmed by the US Senate, which will be controlled by Democrats beginning in January.

This surge occurs as Anthropic prepares for a landmark IPO, highlighting the massive capital deployment and high-leverage competition within the foundational model and AI ecosystem.

news.image_caption: From left: Divesh Makan, Ravi Mhatre, and Yasmin Razavi. (Illustration by Macy Enright for Forbes)
paragraphs: In January 2023, months after OpenAI launched ChatGPT and the world became enamored with AI, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei got a cold email from Iconiq, which started out managing the family offices of the likes of Mark Zuckerberg and Tom Hanks. The firm was interested in investing in the fledgling startup. Iconiq partner Matthew Jacobson and VP Riley Newman met Amodei at Anthropic’s office in San Francisco.

That initial connection blossomed into a historic venture windfall. Iconiq went on to lead Anthropic's $13 billion Series F with a record-setting $3 billion check. In total, Iconiq invested more than $6 billion across Anthropic’s funding rounds, securing an estimated 1.8% equity stake worth approximately $31.8 billion at Thursday's market close—delivering a staggering return exceeding 430% for the firm's strategic partners.

Iconiq isn’t the only venture capital powerhouse reaping massive gains from Anthropic’s public debut. Lightspeed Venture Partners stands as Anthropic's largest financial institutional backer, having poured over $3 billion into the foundation model developer across multiple equity rounds to lock down an equity position exceeding 2%, now valued at well over $35 billion.

Menlo Ventures, which anchored Anthropic’s $750 million Series D round and partnered closely on enterprise distribution of Claude models, deployed more than $1 billion into the company, securing an estimated 1.5% stake worth north of $20 billion. Other major winners include Spark Capital—where general partner Yasmin Razavi led Anthropic's pivotal $450 million Series C at a $5 billion valuation in mid-2023—as well as Coatue Management, Sequoia Capital, and Ashton Kutcher’s Sound Ventures.

Despite the multibillion-dollar windfalls cascading across Silicon Valley venture firms, the largest financial stakes remain concentrated in big tech balance sheets. Strategic cloud partners Amazon and Google hold equity stakes in Anthropic that comfortably eclipse the combined equity holdings of all seven Anthropic co-founders, cementing a new paradigm where cloud compute and hyperscale infrastructure dictate frontier AI cap tables.
paragraphs_zh: 2023年1月，在 OpenAI 推出 ChatGPT 且全球掀起人工智能狂潮数月后，Anthropic 首席执行官达里奥·阿莫代伊收到了一封来自 Iconiq Capital 的引荐邮件。这家以管理超级富豪家族办公室起家的顶级投资机构，对这家初创公司展现出极高兴趣。
这次初见最终演变为风投史上规模空前的投资盛宴。Iconiq 随后领投了 Anthropic 规模达130亿美元的 F 轮融资，累计注资超过60亿美元，锁定约1.8%的股权；以周四收盘价计算，该部分股权价值高达约318亿美元，带来超430%的惊人账面投资回报率。
光速创投（Lightspeed Venture Partners）是 Anthropic 最大规模的纯财务机构股东，累计注资超过30亿美元，锁定超2%的股权份额，当前账面估值已逾350亿美元。
门罗风投（Menlo Ventures）领投 Anthropic 7.5亿美元的 D 轮融资并主导企业级商业化分发，累计投资超10亿美元，持有约1.5%股权。其他主要受益机构还包括早期领投的 Spark Capital、Coatue、红杉资本以及 Sound Ventures。
尽管硅谷风投机构迎来数十亿美元级的历史性分红，但战略级云计算盟友亚马逊与谷歌持有的股权总和已显著超过七位联合创始人所持股权总和，深刻印证了算力军备竞赛时代超大规模基础设施与前沿模型股权结构的高度绑定。

FOR decades, venture capital thrived on small bets that became billion-dollar companies.

Then came Anthropic, rewriting the playbook and forcing investors to write fatter checks to buy stakes at unheard-of valuations.

The artificial intelligence lab’s shares began trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday (Nov 19) at a US$1.5 trillion valuation, delivering multibillion-dollar windfalls to venture

This liquidity event yields massive returns for early backers like Menlo Ventures and Spark Capital, signaling a structural shift in AI venture capital toward large-scale SPV-driven funding models.
paragraphs: Menlo Ventures and Spark Capital are two such firms emerging with some of the biggest returns by multiple
FOR decades, venture capital thrived on small bets that became billion-dollar companies.
Then came Anthropic, rewriting the playbook and forcing investors to write fatter checks to buy stakes at unheard-of valuations.

The artificial intelligence lab’s shares began trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday (Nov 19) at a US$1.5 trillion valuation, delivering multibillion-dollar windfalls to venture investors at a moment when the industry needs fresh liquidity to fund more bets on AI companies.
The stock closed at US$97.17, up 17 per cent from its initial public offering price of US$83.
Anthropic’s stock market value ended the day at about US$1.3 trillion, based on its outstanding shares, or US$1.8 trillion, based on its fully diluted shares.
To join the fundraising frenzy, especially at later stages, venture capital firms invested billions, tapping their own investors for additional capital through special-purpose vehicles.

Find out how enterprises are navigating power constraints and sustainability targets
Menlo Ventures and Spark Capital emerged with some of the biggest returns by multiple.

Spark Capital was the first venture capital firm to lead an Anthropic investment, in a US$450 million Series C round in 2023 at a valuation of US$4.5 billion. Spark general partner Yasmin Razavi, who spearheaded the investment, remains the only investor who sits on Anthropic’s board.

Writing the largest check in the firm’s history, early-stage firm Menlo invested over US$1 billion for a stake of nearly 1.5 per cent, according to a person familiar with the investment. At a US$1.5 trillion market cap, Menlo’s stake is worth over US$20 billion.

To invest beyond the capacity of its existing fund, Menlo raised a US$750 million special-purpose vehicle from limited partners, a tactic that became increasingly common as funding rounds grew, given the capital needs of AI companies.
Sequoia Capital, long known for its early bets, joined a later round and still stands to earn billions of dollars.

Sequoia passed on Anthropic at lower prices. After a leadership change, it wrote its first check at the start of this year, joining a round led by Singapore’s GIC and Coatue at a US$380 billion post-money valuation in February.

It later co-led, alongside Altimeter, Dragoneer and Greenoaks, a round at US$965 billion. Sequoia has invested US$3 billion in Anthropic and continued to invest more through Anthropic’s IPO, signalling further conviction in the AI lab.

Lightspeed Venture Partners, which invested more than US$3 billion in Anthropic, now holds over 2 per cent of the company, making it the largest financial investor in the company, according to two people familiar with the matter.

The returns are possible because of the rapid rise in Anthropic’s valuation and revenue. Its annualised revenue grew from about US$1 billion at the start of 2025 to about US$81 billion last month, as its valuation climbed from US$61.5 billion in March 2025 to US$965 billion in the latest private round this May.
Strategic backers, too, supply much of the unprecedented capital and computing power needed by AI labs. The combined stake of Amazon and Alphabet’s Google in Anthropic is about 28.4 per cent.

Will Griffith, a partner at Iconiq, said: “We’re living through a very unique time of profound change happening at a higher velocity than ever before. The scale of the impact of these businesses and the breadth of market opportunities is larger than anything we’ve seen before.
“And that is going to afford investment opportunities that are larger than what we’ve seen in the past.”
He has invested US$6.1 billion, making the fund the second-largest financial investor by ownership in Anthropic. REUTERS

White House national cyber director Sean Cairncross is leaving his post, Axios has learned.

Why it matters: Cairncross did not want to serve another two years and is leaving now to give the White House time to secure Senate confirmation before Democrats take control in January, two sources said.

The background: Cairncross leads the Office of the National Cyber Director, which coordinates cybersecurity policy and strategy across the federal government.

Case in point: He held technical meetings
news.summary_en: US National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross is stepping down to provide a transition window for his successor to be confirmed by the Senate before Democrats gain control in January. As the head of the Office of the National Cyber Director, Cairncross led federal cybersecurity strategy and notably directed technical reviews of AI firms like Anthropic following commerce-led export control implementations.

news.summary_en: Apple is pivoting its AI strategy by recruiting for a 'Proactive, Agentic AI' engineering lead to develop autonomous systems capable of cross-app interaction, code debugging, and complex task planning. The initiative, integrating teams from Siri, UI Frameworks, and Apple Foundation Models, aims to move beyond static voice commands toward an autonomous agent environment capable of multi-step execution across devices.
paragraphs: Apple is working on its own AI agent that can perform a range of tasks for you, including browsing the web, working across apps, writing code, and calling services. That’s according to a job listing spotted by Bloomberg, which says Apple is looking for an engineer to lead the creation of an agentic AI assistant.

An AI agent from Apple would put the iPhonemaker in the running to compete with the likes of Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dots, Anthropic’s Duet, and Google’s Tasks. Muse, ChatGPT, and Perplexity can already take control of a computer through their Mac apps, while Google just started letting Gemini do the same.

Apple began rolling out its AI-upgraded Siri in September, which you can use to ask questions about what’s on your screen, as well as perform actions across apps. It looks like Apple is planning to give Siri more agentic capabilities, as a report from Bloomberg suggests the company could add the ability to rotate and crop images in Photos, or organize Safari tabs. This lines up with the company’s new job listing, which says the engineer will work closely with teams across its Siri, UI Frameworks, and Apple Foundation Models divisions.

“People already do their most valuable work by moving fluidly between tools: a browser, a document, a terminal, an editor, a service,” the job listing says. “We’re building AI agents that can do the same… These agents plan and carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs, and they can coordinate specialized sub-agents along the way.”

With its upcoming iOS 27.3 update, Apple is also giving developers the ability to integrate Siri AI into “all apps.” This is rolling out as part of a Developer Preview and will eventually allow Siri to perform tasks across a wider range of apps.

paragraphs: Bloomberg reports that Apple is hiring engineers to develop an autonomous AI agent capable of browsing the web, writing code, and controlling apps on behalf of users. Here are the details.
### Apple working on AI agent that can code, browse the web, more

In a report published today, Bloomberg notes that new job listings on Apple’s website indicate the company’s efforts to develop an autonomous AI agent capable of performing complex tasks on the user’s behalf.
Since the breakout success of OpenClaw, autonomous AI agents have become increasingly popular, with companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and SpaceXSI among those offering their own solutions.
The increasing popularity of these agents has put Apple under pressure to catch up, while the company has also introduced new restrictions on how third-party AI agents can access and control Macs.

Last month, Apple announced plans to tighten macOS privacy controls around Full Disk Access, with changes introduced in the macOS 27.3 beta that give users more granular control over which apps and information third-party AI agents can access.

Over at the App Store, Meta’s Muse has become one of the fastest-growing apps in US history, surpassing 10 million downloads in just 40 days, according to Sensor Tower, and spending weeks at the top of the charts. As of today, it sits at No. 2 among free apps, behind TikTok.

And while there are differences in how phone-based and computer-based agents operate, these systems can usually work together, coordinating tasks across devices and apps to accomplish increasingly complex goals.
Back to Bloomberg’s report, it notes Apple recently posted new job listings that offer a closer look at its plans to develop autonomous AI agents:

In one, Apple said it’s seeking a senior engineering manager for a proactive, agentic AI assistant. The system will write code, browse the web, control apps and navigate devices on a user’s behalf, according to the post.
One job listing, which is for “Senior Engineering Manager, Agentic AI – Proactive,” features the following summary:

“Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does. It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple. Our team is building the foundation for that future, and we’re looking for a senior engineering leader to make it real.”

The listing also notes that Apple is building agents that can “plan and carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs, and they can coordinate specialized sub-agents along the way,” much like existing solutions from frontier AI labs.

Today’s report on the new job listings comes just days after Bloomberg reported that Apple wants to make Siri more like an autonomous AI agent, with the ability to proactively carry out tasks without requiring users to initiate every step. According to Mark Gurman, the company could introduce these capabilities as soon as next year.
With the new job listings, Apple has offered a more detailed look at its plans for autonomous AI agents, although the language suggests that development is still in its early stages.

Of course, given how quickly the technology is evolving, the landscape could look very different by the time Apple is ready to introduce its own solution next year, much like how the industry had already moved toward autonomous agents by the time Apple finally launched its long-awaited Siri AI overhaul.

news.summary_en: Nvidia's former CEO Jensen Huang resigned following misconduct allegations, causing the stock to drop nearly 40% from its October 6th peak, despite a record-breaking Q3 revenue of $115.8 billion and the rapid shipment of the Vera Rubin platform. Chairman Harvey Jones has confirmed that the board will not reinstate Huang and has initiated an executive search to stabilize leadership.
paragraphs: “We’ve got this,” Colette Kress, interim CEO of Nvidia, said Tuesday night as she closed out the embattled chip company’s third quarter earnings call.

By Thursday, the company’s stock price was hovering at around $150 per share, a nearly 40 percent drop from its all-time high on October 6th, and wiping out a brief post-earnings pop on Tuesday night. Meanwhile, Wall Street was paying up for one of Nvidia’s biggest customers as Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut at $111.50 per share — 34 percent higher than expected.

Looking at the earnings report numbers alone, Nvidia had a blockbuster quarter. Q3 revenue more than doubled from the same period last year up to total $115.8 billion, driven by data center revenue that was up 110 percent and exceeding Wall Street expectations. Nearly $20 billion in revenue came from the highly anticipated Vera Rubin platform, which shipped during the quarter, becoming the “fastest product ramp in company history,” Kress told investors.

“Our momentum is real,” Kress said. “With the market-leading multiyear roadmap, supply agreements extending through to the end of the decade, and sustainable demand, we are well positioned to accelerate Nvidia’s leadership position.”
But investors are stilltrying to reconcile Nvidia’s stellar recent financial performance and position as a central pillar in the AI economy with serious concerns over its future.

The company’s stock has taken a stunning tumble in recent weeks. Fueled first by a broader market sell-off of chip stocks amid concerns about the AI bubble, the stock took another blow following the resignation of former CEO Jensen Huang amid reports of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy, according to US intelligence sources cited by The New York Times.

Harvey Jones, Nvidia’s newly appointed chairman of the board, told investors on the call Tuesday that the company “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO” and has already tapped an executive search firm to help find a replacement. Huang, who cofounded Nvidia in 1993 and has led the company ever since — famously without a succession plan — has become essentially inseparable from it in the eyes of Wall Street and the media. But while Huang may not be ready to let go, posting on X this week that he’d be “honored” to be reinstated as CEO, Nvidia’s executive suite seems ready to move on.
It has been a tumultuous two and a half weeks for Nvidia.

On October 29th, The New York Times reported that US intelligence agencies believed Jensen Huang to be the target of a Chinese espionage plot. The report centered on his “close relationship” with Alice Huang, a Chinese national and an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company and one of Nvidia’s clients. Nvidia initially contested the report, adding that Jensen Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang “are not unusual or unexpected.”

Nvidia’s stock seemingly remained unaffected by the reports, at least at first. The share price closed at $213.66 on October 29th, down just 0.8 percent from the previous day. (Julian Barnes, one of the reporters on the story, later commented, “I will confess I was kind of surprised that the world’s initial reaction to our October story was a bit muted.”) The stock closed at a 4 percent drop the next day as the entire Nasdaq fell 2.9 percent, the worst single-day decline since June.

The stock continued to fall through Wednesday, November 4th, the day after the blue wave swept the midterms, stoking fears on Wall Street that the new class of Democratic governors in key states like Texas would slow down data center construction. On Thursday, November 5th, Nvidia’s stock fell 9.2 percent, its largest single-day drop in at least a year. But chip stocks began to recover the next day, and by close on Friday, November 6th, Nvidia was back up 2.8 percent to a share price of $186.64.

Then all hell broke loose. On Sunday, November 8th, Jensen Huang sent a company-wide memo to Nvidia staff in which he apologized for engaging in an extramarital affair. The memo coincided with the opening of an independent investigation by Nvidia’s board into Huang’s alleged misconduct and whether company secrets or national security had been compromised. Huang said he would cooperate fully with the investigation. By the opening bell on Monday, November 9th, Nvidia shares had tumbled 7 percent and trading volume surged past its three-month average as investors reacted to the memo. After a brief rebound, the stock continued to oscillate the next day, as more details of Jensen Huang and Alice Huang’s relationship emerged. By the time the market closed on Tuesday, November 10th, Nvidia shares were down to $168.89, nearly 10 percent below the closing price on the last day of 2025.

The stock rebounded slightly on Wednesday, November 11th, as investors prepared for Nvidia’s third quarter earnings call, scheduled for the following Tuesday, November 17th. By Wednesday night, however, shares had plunged yet again as media reports circulated that Nvidia’s board was considering ousting Huang, and other reports emerged detailing a second alleged affair, this time between Huang and an Nvidia employee.

Nvidia announced Huang’s departure on the morning of Thursday, November 12th, sending the company’s shares falling nearly 14 percent at the open. It closed at just a 4.3 percent dip. The intraday low of $148.80 per share was its lowest price in a year.

On December 1st, Jensen Huang will appear before the House Foreign Affairs Committee, the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, and the House Intelligence Committee for transcribed interviews. Nvidia’s general counsel will do the same on December 2nd.

Retail investors have already seized the opportunity to buy the dip. In the first 30 minutes of trading on Thursday, November 12th, retail investors bought $111 million of Nvidia shares in the largest-ever first half-hour of opening for the stock, Bloomberg reported, citing Vanda Research.
They might be onto something.
Nvidia’s average price target is $232.59, with the lowest estimate at $130 and the highest at $350, according to an analysis of analyst projections over the last three months by Google Finance.
Nearly two-thirds of those analysts issued a “Buy” rating for Nvidia in the last three months. Of those, all 30 reiterated that rating post-earnings.
The stock closed at $145.98 on Thursday, a new 52-week low.

Then again, numbers are the core basis for stock market ratings, and numbers may not be Nvidia’s problem right now. It’s everything else — the leadership vacuum, upcoming congressional testimony, regulatory uncertainty, broader questions about neocloud customer financing and sales to China — that will continue to impact the stock in the coming weeks.

news.title: What’s With All These Outages?
news.title_en: What’s With All These Outages?
news.author: Brian Barrett, Leah Feiger, and Sophie Kleeman
news.content_snippet: Microsoft, the FAA, Chase, United, the NSA, and Apple all went down within one week. Officials say none of the outages were cyberattacks, but the internet isn’t buying it. This week on Uncanny Valley, WIRED senior business editor Sophie Kleeman joins Brian Barrett and Leah Feiger to discuss what actually went wrong and why people jumped straight to blaming hackers and AI. Plus, Anthropic’s historic IPO at a reported $1.5 trillion, Nvidia’s first earnings report since Jensen Huang resigned, and t
news.summary_en: Major infrastructure outages occurred sequentially at Microsoft, the FAA, JPMorgan Chase, United Airlines, the NSA, and Apple. Despite official denials of cyberattacks, market anxiety is mounting due to the convergence of these failures with Anthropic's reported $1.5 trillion IPO plans, the first Nvidia earnings report post-Jensen Huang's resignation, and new US executive orders aimed at restricting Chinese entities from accessing AI compute via cloud rentals.
paragraphs: Microsoft, the FAA, Chase, United, the NSA, and Apple all went down within one week. Officials say none of the outages were cyberattacks, but the internet isn’t buying it. This week on Uncanny Valley, WIRED senior business editor Sophie Kleeman joins Brian Barrett and Leah Feiger to discuss what actually went wrong and why people jumped straight to blaming hackers and AI. Plus, Anthropic’s historic IPO at a reported $1.5 trillion, Nvidia’s first earnings report since Jensen Huang resigned, and the administration’s new rule to stop Chinese companies from renting AI chips just before Trump meets Xi.

news.title: Intuit to sell Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for $3.68 billion
news.title_en: Intuit to sell Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for $3.68 billion
news.author: Jordan Novet
news.content_snippet:
Tax software maker Intuit said Thursday that it has agreed to sell marketing subsidiary Mailchimp to Italian technology consolidator Bending Spoons for $3.68 billion in cash and stock. The deal is set to close in early 2027, according to a statement.

The sale is a costly retreat for Intuit, which paid $12 billion for Mailchimp in 2021 in a push beyond its core tax and accounting businesses. Five years later, the software maker is unloading the email-marketing company for less than one-third of
news.summary_en: Intuit has reached an agreement to sell its email-marketing subsidiary Mailchimp to Italian technology consolidator Bending Spoons for $3.68 billion in cash and stock, slated for closure in early 2027. This divestiture, representing a loss of over 70% from the $12 billion acquisition price in 2021, follows Mailchimp's stagnant revenue growth and its role as a drag on Intuit's broader financial valuation.
paragraphs: Tax software maker Intuit said Thursday that it has agreed to sell marketing subsidiary Mailchimp to Italian technology consolidator Bending Spoons for $3.68 billion in cash and stock. The deal is set to close in early 2027, according to a statement.

The sale is a costly retreat for Intuit, which paid $12 billion for Mailchimp in 2021 in a push beyond its core tax and accounting businesses. Five years later, the software maker is unloading the email-marketing company for less than one-third of that price after Mailchimp became a drag on its overall revenue growth.

The deal is the latest instance of Bending Spoons picking up a once promising technology asset. The company bought productivity software startup Airtable in September for 10% of what it was once worth.
The Bending Spoons portfolio also contains AOL, Brightcove, Eventbrite, Evernote, Meetup, Vimeo, and WeTransfer.

In August Intuit started running Mailchimp as a distinct operating segment. The move was meant to give investors more transparency as the company tried to manage the unit for profitability, Sandeep Aujla, Intuit's finance chief, said at a September company briefing.

Also on Thursday, Intuit announced stronger-than-expected earnings and revenue for its fiscal first quarter, which ended on Oct. 31. The company reported $2.91 in adjusted earnings per share on $4.35 billion in revenue. Analysts polled by LSEG were looking for $2.70 per share and $4.31 billion in revenue.
While Intuit's revenue increased 12% year over year, Mailchimp revenue declined 1% to $313 million. Analysts polled by StreetAccount had expected $314.4 million.

Management called for $22.88 to $23.12 in adjusted earnings per share for the 2027 fiscal year, with $23.081 billion to $23.365 billion in revenue. Analysts polled by LSEG had predicted $23.62 in adjusted earnings per share on $23.43 billion in revenue. Intuit shares tumbled 15% in extended trading.

The company said Mailchimp should produce $1.256 billion to $1.266 billion in fiscal 2027 revenue, which would be down 1% to flat year over year. In August Aujla said Intuit anticipated Mailchimp's higher effective prices offsetting increased client churn. Mailchimp was founded in 2001. Rivals include Klaviyo, which went public in 2023.
Berkshire Hathaway invested $600 million in Bending Spoons when the acquirer went public in July, and in October Bending Spoons said Berkshire invested another $330 million.

news.author: Amy Chang Chien
news.content_snippet:
Few things could generate more buzz for a small restaurant than a visit from Jensen Huang. In recent years, the former Nvidia CEO became known for dining out at street markets and hole-in-the-wall noodle joints across Asia, drawing huge crowds of fans and photographers wherever he went.

But after Huang resigned last week amid revelations of multiple extramarital affairs, some of the food vendors he helped put on the map are wondering whether their most famous customer is still good for business
news.summary_en: Jensen Huang has resigned as CEO of Nvidia following allegations of multiple extramarital affairs. The incident has triggered widespread public scrutiny, with small businesses in Taipei weighing the reputational impact of their past association with him against the marketing value of his high-profile visits.
paragraphs: Few things could generate more buzz for a small restaurant than a visit from Jensen Huang. In recent years, the former Nvidia CEO became known for dining out at street markets and hole-in-the-wall noodle joints across Asia, drawing huge crowds of fans and photographers wherever he went.

But after Huang resigned last week amid revelations of multiple extramarital affairs, some of the food vendors he helped put on the map are wondering whether their most famous customer is still good for business. In Taiwan, where Huang was born and his dining habits have long been a spectator sport, many say they aren't ready to turn against their hometown hero.

Tu Chang-chun, the owner of Ice World, a shaved-ice shop in Taipei, describes Huang as friendly, the kind of person who puts others around him at ease. His impression of the billionaire hasn’t changed since he learned of his affair with Alice Huang, a businesswoman accused of spying for China.

“It’s not as if he killed someone or set something on fire. Why blow it all out of proportion?” Tu said on Monday evening, standing beneath the yellow lights of his stall at Linjiang Street Night Market. “Now, a lot of foreigners walk past, see my sign, and laugh. People just love kicking someone when they’re down.”

At the entrance of his shop, Tu continues to proudly display a photo of Huang posing with him and his wife. “I think he’s such a warm and approachable person,” Tu added. “Why are people treating him this way?”
Jensen Huang has visited this shaved ice stall at Taipei’s Linjiang Street Night Market three times since 2023.

Tu says that Huang has visited his shop three times since 2023, and he always orders the same thing: mango shaved ice with tangyuan (sticky rice balls). The dessert, a blend of tropical fruit and condensed milk, is popular in Taipei’s bustling night markets, especially among first-time visitors to the island.
“When he came in for shaved ice, he would spend half an hour eating a single bowl,” recalled Tu. “Whenever someone came up to take a photo with him, he got right up. He’s not pretentious.”

At a tofu pudding shop near Ningxia Night Market in western Taipei, photos of Huang remain on display alongside those of other prominent technology figures who have visited, including Morris Chang, the founder of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC). The store manager, Hsieh, defended the shop’s decision to keep them up.
“I don’t think this changes the fact that he’s a very successful businessman,” Hsieh said of Huang’s affairs with Alice Huang and other women. “Having an affair is a private matter.”

Hsieh, who agreed to be identified only by his surname for privacy reasons, said that Huang had visited the shop four times over the past few years, and on each occasion he seemed friendly and down-to-earth.
Owner Tu Chang-chun said he has no plans to take down photos Jensen Huang visiting his shaved-ice shop.

In Taiwan, Huang’s culinary indulgences extended well beyond street food. He frequented some of Taipei’s most exclusive restaurants, where he hosted technology executives for what became known in the local press as “Trillion-Dollar Banquets,” a reference to the attendees’ combined net worth of more than 1 trillion New Taiwan dollars.

The dinners often drew crowds of journalists and photographers hoping to catch a glimpse of Huang and his guests. The intense media attention helps explain why so many photographs and videos of Huang with Alice Huang were captured in Taiwan. Restaurant owners, meanwhile, welcomed the publicity, often proudly displaying photographs of themselves with Huang inside their establishments.

The Taiwanese tea chain 19 Tea House launched a new drink this week, giving it a name that pokes fun at Huang’s alleged “womanizing” ways. According to the chain, the drink combines osmanthus-infused honey with fresh lemon, offering a blend of fragrant floral notes and sweet-and-tangy citrus flavors.

Support for Huang in Taiwan has also extended far beyond the restaurants he frequented. On Monday evening, Taipei 101, the island’s iconic skyscraper just blocks from one of Huang’s favorite night markets, lit up with messages of support for the former Nvidia CEO, including “Taiwan ♡ Jensen,” “Family ♡ Friendship,” “Thrive Together,” and “Taiwan AI Build Future Together.”

Tech industry figures who supported the initiative told Taiwan’s state-run Central News Agency that the illumination campaign was intended to “help restore Jensen Huang’s reputation,” urging the public not to “kick him when he's down, but instead offer warmth and support during the autumn and winter.”
This is an edition of the Model Behavior newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

news.title: Man hired by Russia spied on Silicon Valley tech and defense company, feds say
news.title_en: Man hired by Russia spied on Silicon Valley tech and defense company, feds say
news.author: Dan Goodin
news.content_snippet:
A Russian national has been indicted on suspicions he was a Russian spy who stalked and surveilled employees of a Silicon Valley company that was assisting Ukraine in its ongoing war with its western neighbor.

Igor D’iu, 25, allegedly photographed the employees and their computer screens as they worked at a coffee shop located near the company’s Palo Alto office, federal prosecutors said Wednesday. He also kept a list of home addresses of employees and a senior executive. At one point, prosecut
news.summary_en: Igor D’iu, a 25-year-old Russian national, has been indicted for espionage after illegally entering the U.S. to surveil employees of a Silicon Valley defense tech firm, widely identified as Palantir. The defendant allegedly gathered intelligence on the company's military support and weapon supply chain to Ukraine.
paragraphs: A Russian national has been indicted on suspicions he was a Russian spy who stalked and surveilled employees of a Silicon Valley company that was assisting Ukraine in its ongoing war with its western neighbor.

Igor D’iu, 25, allegedly photographed the employees and their computer screens as they worked at a coffee shop located near the company’s Palo Alto office, federal prosecutors said Wednesday. He also kept a list of home addresses of employees and a senior executive. At one point, prosecutors said, D’iu trailed an employee as she traveled home from Palo Alto to San Francisco. An affidavit filed in the case referred to the employee as FEMP1, short for female employee, and said the event left her “in a state of emotional distress.”
### Evasive and irregular turns

“FEMP1 made evasive and irregular turns, took back roads, and turned into a grocery store parking lot where D’IU continued aggressively following her vehicle,” an FBI special agent wrote. “D’IU followed FEMP1 through U-turns, illegal left turns, and ran a red light to stay with FEMP1 for nearly thirty miles. FEMP1 called 911 while driving and was instructed to drive directly to San Francisco Police Department (“SFPD”) Mission Station. Near SFPD Mission Station, FEMP1 flagged an SFPD patrol vehicle and reported the incident. D’IU left once FEMP1 made contact with the patrol vehicle.”

When police later questioned D’iu about the incident, the defendant allegedly said he saw a woman get into a car and thought she was “beautiful.” He then told the investigators that he followed her because he “wanted to ask her out on a date.”

Prosecutors didn’t name the company, but both Reuters and Bloomberg, citing unnamed people with knowledge of the case, identified it as Palantir. Ars is unable to confirm that reporting. Palantir representatives didn’t respond to an email seeking confirmation.

D’iu allegedly entered the US unlawfully in the summer of 2026 after being recruited by someone over Telegram. Prosecutors said the party gave D’iu a clandestine assignment to target employees of a large technology and defense company. D’iu received instructions, equipment, and financial support along with information that his work was on behalf of “the motherland.” His instructions were to collect information about the company because it was supplying weapons for use against Russian forces in Ukraine.

Prosecutors said D’iu traveled from Istanbul, Turkey, to Mexico City in June. He then crossed the border into the US and was instructed to buy laptops, cell phones, wireless networking equipment, and remote access software. Besides instructions to monitor company employees at the coffee shop, D’iu’s orders also included positioning his laptop at certain locations near the company so it could be remotely accessed in an attempt to collect information from company employees nearby.

D’iu allegedly obtained fraudulent identification documents to conceal his identity as he conducted his activities. The documents included a falsified California ID card, an altered US passport, and a Social Security card bearing the assumed name of “Hugo Landry Johns.” The passport was allegedly an authentic US passport that originally had been issued to someone elsewhere in the country. It was modified to display D’iu’s photograph and assumed identity.

D’iu was arrested on October 30 and remains in custody. He is charged with one count of Conspiracy to Act as an Agent of a Foreign Government, one count of Acting as an Agent of a Foreign Government Without Notice to the Attorney General, and one count of Interstate Stalking. If convicted for Acting as an Agent of a Foreign Government Without Notice to the Attorney General, he faces a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison, a fine of $250,000, and three years of supervised release. He faces a maximum sentence of five years in prison, a fine of $250,000, and three years of supervised release for each conviction on the other two charges.
D’iu had his initial appearance in federal court on November 2. He is next scheduled to appear in federal court on November 24.

news.summary_en: Meta plans to launch the Muse Charm, a wearable device featuring real-time voice and avatar interaction, at a $300 price point by this December. paragraphs: Meta is planning to price the Muse Charm, a little gadget with a screen that lets you chat with your Muse AI agent, at $300, according to The Information. CEO Mark Zuckerberg revealed the gadget earlier this year and said the company expected to ship the Charm “in time for the holidays in December,” but he didn’t provide a price at the time.

When he announced the Muse Charm, Zuckerberg said that the company had “packed the whole Muse experience,” including real-time voice and avatar technology, into the gadget. It has a fingerprint sensor, and you can tap it to be able to talk to a Muse AI agent without unlocking a phone or opening an app. The Information reports that the Muse Charm will come with a free 12-month 5G data plan from Verizon.

Spokesperson Tyler Yee wrote to The Information that “We’re charmed by the interest in our AI devices, and we’ll have more to share soon.” When reached for comment by The Verge, Yee provided the same statement.
The company is also working on a smartwatch, The Information says, but a launch for that has been pushed to 2027 as Meta tries to get Muse Charm out the door.
Meta also open sourced code to let users make their own Muse gadgets, which my colleague Sean Hollister used to make his own DIY Muse Charm.

paragraphs: Google is updating its homepage to include AI searches. In a post on X, Google’s vice president of product, Robby Stein, shows how you can now open a collapsible sidebar to view and continue your AI chats.

Based on the GIF shared by Stein, it looks like you can open the sidebar by clicking the gray bar that appears on the left side of your screen. From there, Google will show a list of the searches you’ve made using AI Mode, along with the ability to start a new thread, search your threads, or connect a Gemini Notebook.

It’s yet another big change for Google’s homepage, which has long presented you with a single bar to kick off your web search. The company brought its AI Mode button to its search bar last year, which opens up a chatbot-like search experience within Google. In May, Google updated its search box to accommodate longer queries and added AI-powered autocomplete.

Stein says Google is rolling out the option because “people are coming to Search with more questions that aren’t just one and done,” adding that “in testing, this sidebar made a big difference for making progress & continuing to explore the web.” The new homepage is rolling out globally on desktop.
